stem: Which interface command sets the OSPF cost of a single link to 100 without changing the cost of any other interface?
explanation: auto-cost reference-bandwidth is a router-wide setting, so it changes every interface's cost at once. ip ospf cost applies to one interface only and takes precedence over the value derived from reference bandwidth and interface bandwidth.

choices.text: ip ospf cost 100
auto-cost reference-bandwidth 100
ospf cost 100
bandwidth 100000

stem: What OSPF network type is assigned by default to a point-to-point serial interface running HDLC?
explanation: Cisco treats a point-to-point link as having exactly one possible neighbour, so it defaults to the point-to-point network type. No DR or BDR election happens and hellos are sent every 10 seconds.

choices.text: Point-to-point
Broadcast
Non-broadcast
Point-to-multipoint

stem: Why does OSPF advertise a loopback interface as a /32 host route?
explanation: A loopback is given the loopback network type, which OSPF treats as a stub host rather than a shared segment. Advertising it as /32 makes the address reachable from anywhere in the domain without implying that a subnet sits behind it.

choices.text: Because the loopback network type advertises it as a stub host
Because loopback interfaces cannot be configured with a prefix shorter than /32
Because OSPF summarises every loopback into 0.0.0.0/0
Because the DR rewrites loopback prefixes as host LSAs

stem: Which command makes OSPF treat an NBMA interface as a broadcast medium so a DR election takes place?
explanation: Non-broadcast networks send hellos as unicast and elect a DR only on a fully meshed topology. ip ospf network broadcast makes OSPF behave as if the segment supports multicast, so hellos and DR election work as they do on Ethernet — although the medium still has to carry those multicast frames.

choices.text: ip ospf network broadcast
ip ospf network non-broadcast
ip ospf priority 1
ip ospf dr-election enable

stem: Which OSPF network type behaves like point-to-multipoint but requires explicit neighbour statements because the medium cannot carry multicast hellos?
explanation: Point-to-multipoint sends hellos as multicast, which a Frame Relay or ATM hub cannot replicate to every spoke. The non-broadcast variant keeps the /32 host-route advertisement of point-to-multipoint but needs neighbour commands so the hub can unicast hellos to each spoke individually.

choices.text: Point-to-multipoint non-broadcast
Non-broadcast (NBMA)
Point-to-point
Broadcast

stem: Why must every non-backbone OSPF area touch area 0, or reach it through a virtual link?
explanation: Inter-area prefixes are only exchanged through the backbone, so an area with no path to area 0 has no way to receive Type 3 LSAs from any other area. That two-level hierarchy is also what prevents inter-area routing loops, since an area can never learn a prefix from a peer area without it passing through the backbone.

choices.text: Because inter-area LSAs are only exchanged through the backbone, which keeps inter-area routing loop-free
Because only area 0 routers are permitted to run the SPF algorithm
Because area 0 is the only area that can authenticate OSPF packets
Because a non-backbone area may contain only one ABR

stem: Which OSPF LSA type is generated by the DR on a multi-access segment to represent that segment and the routers attached to it?
explanation: Type 1 router LSAs describe each router individually. The Type 2 network LSA is generated by the DR and models the shared segment as a pseudonode, and every other router on the segment references that pseudonode in its own Type 1 LSA so the topology tree collapses the segment into a single node.

choices.text: Type 2 network LSA
Type 1 router LSA
Type 3 summary LSA
Type 5 external LSA

stem: What distinguishes an OSPF not-so-stubby area from a normal stub area?
explanation: A stub area refuses Type 5 externals entirely. An NSSA keeps that restriction toward the backbone but lets an ASBR inside the area originate external prefixes as Type 7 LSAs, which the ABR then translates into Type 5 when flooding them into the rest of the domain.

choices.text: An ASBR inside the area may inject external routes as Type 7 LSAs
Type 5 LSAs are allowed to flood through it unchanged
It removes the requirement to connect to area 0
It disables DR election on all of its segments

stem: Which two behaviours define an OSPF stub area?
explanation: A stub area blocks Type 5 external LSAs at its border, so routers inside carry a much smaller database. The ABR compensates by injecting a default route, which keeps external destinations reachable even though the external prefixes themselves never enter the area.

choices.text: It blocks Type 5 LSAs and receives a default route from the ABR
It blocks Type 3 LSAs and receives a default route from the ASBR
It blocks Type 1 and Type 2 LSAs within the area
It blocks every LSA and relies on static routes instead

stem: Which IPv6 multicast address does OSPFv3 use for hellos addressed to the DR and BDR?
explanation: FF02::5 reaches every OSPFv3 router on the link, while FF02::6 is the all-DR/BDR group. The DR joins both groups, so it receives the same hello a DROTHER sends to the general group and the adjacency survives the election.

stem: Which addresses do OSPFv3 neighbours use as the source and destination of their hello packets?
explanation: OSPFv3 runs per link rather than per subnet, so it uses the link-local address of the outgoing interface as the source and a link-local multicast group as the destination. Global prefixes are carried inside LSAs but are not needed to build the adjacency.

choices.text: The link-local addresses of the participating interfaces
The global unicast addresses of the participating interfaces
The 32-bit router ID of each neighbour
The unique-local addresses configured on the loopbacks

stem: How is OSPFv3 authentication implemented?
explanation: OSPFv2 carries its own authentication fields in the packet header. OSPFv3 removed them and relies on IPsec instead — AH for integrity, ESP for confidentiality — applied per interface, which lets the same mechanisms protect OSPFv3 as any other IPv6 traffic.

choices.text: Through IPsec AH or ESP applied to the interface
Through MD5 keys configured under the OSPFv3 process
Through a plaintext password carried in each hello packet
Through a shared key carried inside the Type 1 router LSA

stem: Which OSPFv3 LSA carries a router's link-local address and the prefixes associated with one link to the neighbours on that link?
explanation: OSPFv3 split OSPFv2's router LSA into pieces. Type 8 describes a single link, including the link-local address the neighbours need and any prefixes on it, and its scope is the link itself, so it is never flooded beyond the routers attached to that segment.

choices.text: Type 8 link LSA
Type 9 intra-area-prefix LSA
Type 1 router LSA
Type 5 external LSA

stem: In EIGRP, what is the reported distance of a route?
explanation: The reported distance, also called the advertised distance, is the metric the neighbour claims for the destination. EIGRP compares it with the local feasible distance to decide whether the neighbour offers a loop-free backup — a neighbour whose reported distance is higher than the current feasible distance is not trusted as a feasible successor.

choices.text: The metric the neighbour advertises for the destination
The metric this router computes for its own best path
The number of hops between the two routers
The administrative distance assigned to the EIGRP process

stem: What are the default EIGRP hello and hold timers on a link of T1 speed or faster?
explanation: EIGRP scales its timers to link speed: 5-second hellos with a 15-second hold on links faster than T1, and 60/180 on slower multipoint links. The longer timers on slow links avoid wasting WAN capacity on hellos at the cost of slower failure detection.

choices.text: 5 seconds hello, 15 seconds hold
10 seconds hello, 40 seconds hold
30 seconds hello, 120 seconds hold
60 seconds hello, 180 seconds hold

stem: Which IP protocol number does EIGRP use?
explanation: EIGRP is not carried over TCP or UDP. It runs directly over IP with protocol number 88, which is why an ACL that filters only TCP and UDP can silently break EIGRP adjacencies.

stem: Which two components contribute to the EIGRP composite metric by default?
explanation: By default EIGRP sets K1 and K3 to one, so only bandwidth and delay are used. Load and reliability can be added by changing the K-values, but every router in the AS must use identical values or neighbours will disagree about which path is best; MTU is carried in updates but never used in the calculation.

choices.text: Bandwidth and delay
Bandwidth and hop count
Delay and load
Reliability and MTU

stem: What does the OSPF DOWN state mean for a neighbour?
explanation: DOWN means no hello has been received from that neighbour within the dead interval, or none has ever arrived. It is the starting state before any adjacency exists, and a neighbour permanently stuck there points to a one-way path, a mismatched area, or a passive interface.

choices.text: No hello has been received from the neighbour
Hellos are exchanged but the databases are still synchronising
The neighbour is a DROTHER and will never become adjacent
The neighbour has finished the database exchange

stem: Which OSPF neighbour state means link-state requests have been sent and the router is waiting for the matching updates?
explanation: In LOADING the router has finished the database description exchange and knows exactly which LSAs it is missing. It sends link-state requests and waits for the replies, so a neighbour stuck here usually means a requested LSA cannot be retrieved.

choices.text: LOADING
EXCHANGE
EXSTART
FULL

stem: What does the OSPF FULL state signify?
explanation: FULL means the two routers hold identical link-state databases for the area and can forward traffic through each other. On a broadcast segment only the DR and BDR reach FULL with every other router, while DROTHERs stay at 2-WAY with each other by design.

choices.text: The databases are synchronised and traffic can be forwarded through the neighbour
The routers are still comparing database description packets
The routers have exchanged hellos but no database information
The routers have agreed on a DR but not on their area IDs

stem: A router learns four equal-cost OSPF paths to the same prefix. What does Cisco IOS do by default?
explanation: Equal-cost paths are all installed in the routing table and traffic is load-balanced across them, up to the default maximum of four. The maximum-paths command changes that limit; any path beyond it stays out of the table rather than being used as a standby.

choices.text: It installs up to four paths and load-balances across them
It installs only the first path learned and discards the rest
It installs all four but forwards only along the lowest router ID
It rejects the prefix until the tie is broken manually

stem: In `show ip route` output, what does a route marked `S*` represent?
explanation: The asterisk flags the route as a candidate default. A static default route therefore appears as S*: the S says static, and the star says this is the entry the router will use when no more specific match exists.

choices.text: A static route that is a candidate default
A static route that has been redistributed into a routing protocol
A static route that is currently inactive
A summary static route covering several prefixes

stem: A new router joins an OSPF broadcast segment with a higher interface priority than the current DR. What happens?
explanation: OSPF does not preempt. The existing DR keeps the role until it fails or the OSPF process is cleared, so the new router waits as a DROTHER no matter how high its priority is.

choices.text: Nothing; the current DR keeps the role until it fails or the process is cleared
The new router immediately becomes DR and the old DR becomes BDR
Both routers become DR and share the pseudonode
The segment re-runs the election and all adjacencies drop to DOWN

stem: How often does an OSPF router refresh its self-originated LSAs, and why?
explanation: Every 30 minutes the originator re-floods each of its LSAs with a fresh sequence number even when nothing has changed. That periodic refresh is what allows a stale LSA to age out eventually — without it, a crashed router's information could persist forever.

choices.text: Every 30 minutes, so the sequence number keeps advancing and stale copies can age out
Every 5 minutes, to resynchronise the database after each SPF run
Every 60 minutes, when the LSA reaches max age
Only when the topology changes, because unchanged LSAs are never re-sent

stem: Which command shows the area, network type, timers, and cost configured for each OSPF-enabled interface?
explanation: show ip ospf neighbor only tells you who is adjacent. show ip ospf interface shows the local side of each link — area ID, network type, hello and dead intervals, cost, and DR/BDR roles — which is what you need when two routers refuse to become neighbours.

choices.text: show ip ospf interface
show ip ospf neighbor
show ip ospf database
show ip protocols

stem: Two routers sit in the same area, on the same subnet, with matching timers, yet the adjacency never leaves DOWN. Both have OSPF authentication configured. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: OSPF discards hellos whose authentication does not match, so the neighbour never appears at all — not even in INIT. A key or authentication-type mismatch is invisible in the neighbour table because the packets are dropped before they are recorded.

choices.text: The authentication type or key does not match on the two interfaces
The two routers are using different OSPF process IDs
The DR election has not completed yet
One router has a lower OSPF priority than the other

stem: What are the default BGP KEEPALIVE interval and hold time?
explanation: BGP sends a KEEPALIVE every 60 seconds by default and declares the peer dead after 180 seconds without one, so the hold time is three times the keepalive. If the two peers advertise different hold times, the lower value is used.

choices.text: 60 seconds keepalive, 180 seconds hold
30 seconds keepalive, 90 seconds hold
10 seconds keepalive, 40 seconds hold
180 seconds keepalive, 540 seconds hold

stem: Why is it best practice to specify both the exit interface and the next-hop address in a static route over a multi-access Ethernet link?
explanation: With only an exit interface on Ethernet, the router must ARP for every individual destination address it forwards to. Adding the next hop makes it resolve one gateway address and reuse that frame rewrite.

choices.text: It avoids resolving every destination individually with ARP on that interface
It lowers the administrative distance of the route
It keeps the route installed when the interface goes down
It allows the route to be redistributed into OSPF

stem: Which OSPF LSA type is originated only by a designated router on a broadcast multi-access network?
explanation: The Type 2 network LSA describes the multi-access segment and the routers attached to it, and only the DR for that segment generates it.

choices.text: Type 2 network LSA
Type 1 router LSA
Type 3 summary LSA
Type 5 external LSA

stem: An interface is configured with `passive-interface` under the OSPF process. What is the effect on that interface?
explanation: A passive interface still has its network advertised into OSPF, but no hellos are sent and no adjacency forms. It is the standard way to advertise a stub or user-facing subnet.

choices.text: The network is still advertised but no hellos are sent and no adjacency forms
The interface is removed from OSPF and its network is no longer advertised
The interface stops forwarding all user traffic
The interface is converted into an OSPF stub network type

stem: Which BGP path-selection attribute is evaluated first on a Cisco router?
explanation: Cisco evaluates weight before every other attribute. A locally significant value, it is checked first and the highest weight wins before local preference is even considered.

choices.text: Weight
Local preference
AS path length
Multi-exit discriminator

stem: Which condition must a neighbour's reported distance satisfy before that neighbour can qualify as an EIGRP feasible successor?
explanation: The feasibility condition requires the reported distance to be lower than the current feasible distance. That inequality is what guarantees the backup path cannot loop back through the router itself.

choices.text: Its reported distance must be lower than the current feasible distance
Its reported distance must equal the current feasible distance
Its reported distance must be lower than the successor's reported distance
Its reported distance must be lower than the configured interface bandwidth

stem: Which single prefix summarises the contiguous networks 10.10.8.0/24 through 10.10.15.0/24?
explanation: Eight consecutive /24 networks span 2048 addresses, which is one /21. The first address 10.10.8.0 is aligned on a /21 boundary, so 10.10.8.0/21 covers the whole range.

stem: What does the line 'Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0' indicate in `show ip route` output?
explanation: It reports that a default route is installed. The router uses it only for destinations that no more specific entry matches, so it never overrides longer prefixes.

choices.text: A default route is installed and used when no more specific route matches
The router currently has no routes in its table
The router is using 203.0.113.1 as its OSPF router ID
All traffic is sent to 203.0.113.1, overriding more specific routes

stem: R1 learns 10.7.0.0/16 from OSPF with metric 20 and from internal EIGRP with metric 2,170,112. Which route is installed in the routing table?
explanation: Administrative distance is compared before metric, and metrics from different protocols are not comparable. Internal EIGRP at 90 beats OSPF at 110 regardless of the metric values.

choices.text: The EIGRP route, because its administrative distance of 90 beats OSPF's 110
The OSPF route, because metric 20 is far lower than 2,170,112
Both routes, and the router load-balances across them
Neither, because the two metrics are not comparable

stem: What is the main scalability limitation of router-on-a-stick inter-VLAN routing?
explanation: Every VLAN shares a single physical link and a single router interface, so all inter-VLAN traffic competes for the same bandwidth and the router forwards it in software.

choices.text: All inter-VLAN traffic for every VLAN shares one physical link and one router interface
It supports only two VLANs per subinterface
It cannot carry 802.1Q tags longer than four bytes
It requires a separate routing protocol for each VLAN

stem: A floating static route resolves its next hop through the very route it is meant to back up. Why is that a problem?
explanation: If the backup's next hop is only reachable through the primary path, losing that path makes the next hop unresolvable, so the backup route is withdrawn at the same moment it is needed.

choices.text: When the primary path fails the next hop becomes unreachable, so the backup disappears too
The router refuses to install a static route whose next hop is learned dynamically
The backup inherits the primary route's administrative distance
The router load-balances between the two routes instead of preferring one

stem: A static IPv6 route points at next hop 2001:db8:10::5, which already falls inside a connected subnet. How does the router treat that next hop?
explanation: A next hop that sits inside a connected prefix is on-link, so the router resolves its MAC with neighbour discovery and forwards without another table lookup. An off-link next hop would instead need a separate more specific route to resolve it first.

choices.text: As an on-link neighbour that neighbour discovery resolves, with no further lookup
As an off-link address that needs a recursive lookup through another route
As a link-local address that must be paired with an exit interface
As unusable, because static next hops must always be link-local

stem: How is an IPv6 default route injected into OSPFv3?
explanation: OSPFv3 does not originate a default route on its own. The `default-information originate` command under the OSPFv3 process advertises ::/0, optionally only while a default route already exists locally.

choices.text: With default-information originate under the OSPFv3 process
With a static ::/0 route, which OSPFv3 redistributes automatically
By enabling ipv6 unicast-routing on the area border router
OSPFv3 always floods a default route from the designated router

stem: What are the default OSPF hello and dead intervals on an NBMA network type?
explanation: NBMA uses 30-second hellos and a 120-second dead interval, four times longer than the 10 and 40 seconds used on broadcast and point-to-point links. Mismatched timers prevent adjacency formation.

choices.text: 30 seconds and 120 seconds
10 seconds and 40 seconds
5 seconds and 20 seconds
60 seconds and 240 seconds

stem: Two OSPF routers remain stuck in the ExStart state. What is the most common cause?
explanation: ExStart is where the master and slave agree on the initial database description sequence number, and that exchange is sensitive to MTU. A mismatched interface MTU makes the larger DBD packet fail, so the state never advances.

choices.text: A mismatched interface MTU between the two routers
A mismatched OSPF process ID on the two routers
Different OSPF router IDs on the same segment
One router configured as a stub area and the other as normal

stem: An OSPF neighbour is stuck permanently in the INIT state. What does that tell you?
explanation: INIT means the local router has received a hello but does not see its own router ID listed in it. Hellos are therefore arriving one way only, which points to a filter, a one-way path, or a multicast problem.

choices.text: Hellos are arriving in one direction only, so the local router never sees itself in the neighbour's hello
The two routers disagree on the area ID
The neighbour is a DROTHER and must stay in INIT by design
The database description exchange has not started yet

stem: How many OSPFv3 adjacencies form on an interface that has three global IPv6 prefixes, and what addresses carry them?
explanation: OSPFv3 runs over the link-local address and is effectively per-link rather than per-prefix, so a single adjacency forms. The global prefixes are carried inside the LSAs rather than driving separate sessions.

choices.text: One adjacency, sourced from the link-local addresses of the two routers
Three adjacencies, one per global prefix
Two adjacencies, one per address family
One adjacency per prefix pair, negotiated by the designated router

stem: How does the forwarding table differ from the routing table?
explanation: The routing table is the routing protocol's view, holding all candidate routes and their attributes. The forwarding table, or FIB, is the distilled result optimised for line-rate lookup: one best next hop per destination prefix.

choices.text: The routing table holds all candidate routes, while the forwarding table holds only the selected best next hop per prefix
The routing table holds only connected routes, while the forwarding table holds learned routes
The forwarding table holds every route and the routing table holds only the default route
They are identical, and the names simply differ by platform

stem: What is a recursive route lookup?
explanation: When a route names a next hop rather than an exit interface, the router looks that next hop up in the table again to find how to reach it. The recursion ends at a route with a directly connected next hop.

choices.text: Looking up the next-hop address in the table again to find the real exit interface
Re-reading the routing table every time a packet arrives
Querying a neighbour for a route it has already advertised
Recomputing the shortest path tree after every topology change

stem: Two routes exist for a destination: 10.1.0.0/16 learned from OSPF and 10.1.4.0/24 learned from EIGRP. Which is used for traffic to 10.1.4.9?
explanation: Administrative distance only compares routes for the same prefix. Because the destination falls inside both prefixes, the router first chooses the longest match, which is the /24, regardless of protocol.

choices.text: The EIGRP /24, because the longest matching prefix wins before distance is considered
The OSPF /16, because OSPF has the lower administrative distance of the two
Neither, because the overlapping prefixes make the destination unreachable
Both, and the router load-balances across the two paths

stem: In an HSRP group, what address do hosts use as their default gateway?
explanation: The virtual address belongs to the group, not to either router, so hosts never need reconfiguration when the active role moves. Each router still keeps its own physical address for management.

choices.text: The shared virtual IP address
The active router's physical interface address
The standby router's physical interface address
The HSRP group multicast address

stem: What does HSRP object tracking accomplish?
explanation: Tracking ties group priority to the health of something else, usually the uplink. When the tracked object fails the priority drops below the peer's, and preemption hands the active role to the router that can still forward.

choices.text: It lowers a router's priority, and thus its chance of staying active, when a tracked interface or object fails
It raises the hello timer when the uplink is congested
It synchronizes the HSRP group with a VRRP group
It authenticates HSRP hello messages

stem: What does a totally stubby OSPF area block that an ordinary stub area does not?
explanation: A stub area filters type 5 externals but still learns inter-area summaries. A totally stubby area also filters type 3 summaries, leaving a single default route toward area 0.

choices.text: Type 3 summary LSAs in addition to the external LSAs a stub already blocks
Only type 1 and type 2 LSAs
Type 5 LSAs while still allowing type 3 summaries
All LSAs of every type, including the default route

stem: What does a type 1 OSPF LSA describe?
explanation: Every OSPF router floods one router LSA per area describing its own interfaces and link states. Type 2 covers the multi-access segment, type 3 carries inter-area prefixes, and type 5 carries externals.

choices.text: The originating router's links, interfaces, and their costs within one area
The set of routers attached to a multi-access segment
Networks reachable in other areas of the same domain
Routes redistributed from outside the OSPF domain

stem: Which command explicitly sets a router's OSPF router ID?
explanation: The router-id command under router ospf pins the identifier, which otherwise comes from the highest loopback address or the highest active physical address. A fixed ID keeps adjacencies stable when interfaces change.

choices.text: router-id 10.255.255.1 under the OSPF process
ospf router-id 10.255.255.1 on each interface
ip ospf id 10.255.255.1 in global configuration

stem: Which interface command changes how often OSPF sends hello packets on a single link?
explanation: The hello interval is an interface-level OSPF setting, so it is applied with ip ospf hello-interval. Both neighbours must agree on the value or the adjacency will not form.

choices.text: ip ospf hello-interval 5
ospf hello 5
ip hello-interval ospf 5
timers hello 5

stem: What is the default administrative distance of a RIP route?
explanation: Cisco assigns RIP an administrative distance of 120, which places it below OSPF at 110 and EIGRP at 90. That ordering is why a router prefers almost any other protocol over RIP for the same prefix.

stem: Which BGP neighbour state means the TCP session is up and an OPEN message has been sent but not yet answered?
explanation: OpenSent follows a successful TCP handshake, when the local router has transmitted its OPEN and is waiting for the peer's. Receiving that OPEN moves the session to OpenConfirm, and a KEEPALIVE completes it as Established.

choices.text: OpenSent
Idle
Established
Connect

stem: What administrative distance does Cisco assign to an EIGRP summary route?
explanation: A summary generated by the local router is preferred over any other source, so it is given an administrative distance of 5. Internal EIGRP routes use 90 and external ones 170.

stem: Why is a floating static route made to lose by raising its administrative distance rather than its metric?
explanation: A static route and an OSPF route are not comparable by metric because the numbers mean different things. Administrative distance is the cross-protocol tiebreak, so raising it is what keeps the static route out of the table until the dynamic route disappears.

choices.text: Administrative distance decides between routes from different sources, while metrics are only compared within one protocol
Static routes have no metric field at all
A higher metric would make the route preferred
Metrics only apply to IPv6 routes

stem: Why must an IPv6 static route that uses a link-local next hop also specify the outgoing interface?
explanation: Link-local addresses are only unique within a single link, so the router cannot tell which interface to use from the address alone. Supplying the exit interface makes the route fully specified and removes the ambiguity.

choices.text: A link-local address is only unique on one link, so the exit interface is required
IPv6 does not support next-hop addresses in static routes
The interface is needed only when the next hop is a global address
Without it the route becomes a default route

stem: What is the default administrative distance of a static route that points to a next-hop address?
explanation: A static route with a specified next hop is trusted almost completely and carries AD 1. Only a directly connected route at AD 0 is preferred over it.

stem: How does the forwarding information base differ from the routing information base on a router?
explanation: The RIB is the control-plane table holding every candidate route learned from connected networks, statics, and routing protocols along with their metrics and distances. The FIB is the derived data-plane table containing only the selected best route for each prefix, and it is what actually drives packet forwarding.

choices.text: The RIB holds all candidate routes; the FIB holds only the selected best paths used for forwarding
The RIB holds only connected routes; the FIB holds learned routes
The FIB is populated before the RIB during convergence
The RIB is used for IPv6 and the FIB for IPv4

stem: What does the command show ip route ospf display?
explanation: The command filters the routing table to entries whose source is OSPF, showing the OSPF code, the advertising router, and the metric. Connected and static routes are omitted.

choices.text: Only routes learned through OSPF
The full OSPF link-state database
Only OSPF neighbor adjacencies
All routes including connected and static

stem: Which command creates a switched virtual interface for VLAN 10?
explanation: The interface vlan 10 command enters SVI configuration, where an IP address can be assigned to provide routing or management access for that VLAN. The SVI is the Layer 3 presence of the VLAN on the switch.

choices.text: interface vlan 10
interface gigabitethernet0/1.10
vlan 10 interface
switchport access vlan 10

stem: An SVI is configured with an IP address and no shutdown, yet it stays down/down. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: An SVI only comes up when at least one port in that VLAN is up and forwarding, or when the VLAN itself is active on the switch. Without a live access port or trunk carrying the VLAN, there is nothing to bring the interface up.

choices.text: No active port is assigned to that VLAN
The SVI needs a default gateway configured
The VLAN must be created with the vlan database command
An SVI cannot carry an IPv4 address

stem: Which command enables OSPFv3 process 1 on a router?
explanation: OSPFv3 is configured through the ipv6 router ospf process command, then interfaces are enabled with ipv6 ospf 1 area under each interface. OSPFv3 runs over IPv6 and uses link-local addresses for adjacencies.

choices.text: ipv6 router ospf 1
router ospf 1
router ipv6 ospf 1
ospfv3 1 enable

stem: Two routers have OSPFv3 configured on a shared link but form no adjacency. The area IDs match and the link is up. What should be checked next?
explanation: OSPFv3 requires the per-interface instance ID to match between neighbours; a mismatch means the packets belong to different OSPFv3 instances and are ignored. Unlike OSPFv2, the process ID is local, but the interface instance ID must agree.

choices.text: The OSPFv3 instance ID on both interfaces
The OSPFv2 process ID on both routers
The IPv4 subnet mask on the link

stem: Which single summary route covers 192.168.0.0/24 through 192.168.3.0/24?
explanation: The four /24 networks share the first 22 bits, so they aggregate into 192.168.0.0/22. That block spans 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.3.255 and replaces four separate advertisements with one.

stem: On an OSPF ASBR, which command summarizes redistributed external routes before they are advertised into the OSPF domain?
explanation: The summary-address command is applied in router configuration on the ASBR and creates a single aggregate for a range of external prefixes. Internal area summarization instead uses the area range command on an ABR.

choices.text: summary-address
area range
ip summary-address eigrp
auto-summary

stem: Two OSPF routers are connected by a working link but are configured in different areas. What is the result?
explanation: OSPF requires both ends of a link to agree on the area ID before they can become neighbours. A mismatch keeps them from progressing past the initial hello exchange, so no adjacency forms and no routes are exchanged.

choices.text: No adjacency forms because the area IDs must match on the link
The routers become neighbours but exchange no Type 1 LSAs
The link is treated as an external connection automatically
The router with the higher router ID becomes the ABR

stem: On a broadcast multi-access OSPF segment, a router shows a neighbour stuck in 2WAY/DROTHER. Is this a fault?
explanation: On broadcast and NBMA networks, routers that are neither the DR nor the BDR stay in 2WAY with each other by design. Only a neighbour that should be DR or BDR remaining in 2WAY, or a point-to-point link showing it, indicates a problem.

choices.text: No; non-DR and non-BDR routers stay in 2WAY on broadcast segments by design
Yes; every neighbour must reach FULL
Yes; it means the hello timers differ
No; 2WAY means the neighbour is the DR
